hook: Universal Music says one account name released 4,562 tracks through DistroKid in twelve months.
payoff: The case targets responsibility of the distribution pipe; 4,562 remains an allegation and there is no merits ruling.

hook: DistroKid is not Spotify. It primarily markets itself as the distribution pipe in between.
payoff: The legal/business question is what happens when a high-scale distributor receives a rights conflict.

hook: The most important sentence in Universal's complaint may be the one explaining what this lawsuit is not about.
payoff: The complaint does not frame clearly disclosed AI music itself as illegal; the dispute centers alleged infringement/deception and distributor conduct.

hook: UMG's complaint points to 1,000 examples and says its investigation had identified nearly 2,000 allegedly infringing recordings.
payoff: The numbers show the scale of UMG's theory, not 1,000 or 2,000 court findings.

hook: One of the strangest parts of the lawsuit is a code most listeners never see: the ISRC.
payoff: Distribution moves identifying metadata as well as audio; UMG's ISRC misuse theory remains an allegation and metadata conflict alone does not prove infringement.

hook: The lawsuit gets more serious at the moment UMG says DistroKid was told there was a rights conflict.
payoff: The question shifts to alleged post-notice conduct; Universal's account remains unadjudicated.

hook: DistroKid says Universal's version of the story is wrong.
payoff: DistroKid points to safeguards and rules, but policy alone does not resolve the conduct UMG alleges.

hook: You can create a fake nine-figure headline from this lawsuit with one multiplication. That would be misleading.
payoff: $150,000 per work is only a discretionary statutory ceiling if willfulness is proved and found; no award or fixed aggregate case value exists.
